This is a demo post showing what Quarto can do — LaTeX, code, and plots in one place.

## The attention formula

Given queries $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times d_k}$ and keys $K \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times d_k}$, the attention pattern is:

$$A = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)$$

The $\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling prevents the dot products from growing large when $d_k$ is big, which would push softmax into saturation (near-zero gradients).

For a single query vector $q$ and key matrix $K$, the score for position $j$ is:

$$a_j = \frac{\exp(q \cdot k_j / \sqrt{d_k})}{\sum_{i} \exp(q \cdot k_i / \sqrt{d_k})}$$

## Computing it by hand

Let's say $d_k = 2$ and we have 3 tokens with:

$$Q = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad K = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

The raw scores $QK^\top / \sqrt{2}$:

$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$

Row 3 (token 3) attends most strongly to itself — its query $(1,1)$ aligns best with key $(1,1)$.

## In code

```{python}
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Q = torch.tensor([[1., 0.], [0., 1.], [1., 1.]])
K = torch.tensor([[1., 0.], [0., 1.], [1., 1.]])

d_k = Q.shape[-1]
scores = Q @ K.T / d_k**0.5
attn = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)

print("Attention pattern:")
print(attn.round(decimals=3))
```

## Visualizing the pattern

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 3))
im = ax.imshow(attn.numpy(), cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=1)
ax.set_xticks([0,1,2]); ax.set_xticklabels(["tok 1","tok 2","tok 3"])
ax.set_yticks([0,1,2]); ax.set_yticklabels(["tok 1","tok 2","tok 3"])
ax.set_xlabel("Key"); ax.set_ylabel("Query")
ax.set_title("Attention pattern")
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The diagonal dominance means each token attends most to itself — makes sense since $Q = K$ here. In a real transformer the weights learned to make $Q \neq K$, which is where interesting structure emerges.
